analysis.one_liner: Creates a government-run public health insurance option sold alongside private plans on the ACA exchanges.
analysis.headline: Backed by 12 Senate Democrats, the public-option bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee and never received a markup, vote, or floor action before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would create a Medicare-administered health plan that individuals and small businesses could buy on the ACA exchanges instead of a private plan. It would roll out first in areas with little insurer competition, provider shortages, or rural high costs, reaching everywhere by 2024, with providers paid at Medicare rates (up to 25% higher in rural areas). It would also expand ACA premium subsidies to families above four times the poverty level, let the government negotiate Medicare drug prices, and set up a $10 billion-a-year reinsurance program to lower individual-market premiums.
analysis.who_benefits: People buying their own health coverage, especially in rural areas or markets with only one insurer, would get a lower-cost public alternative; small businesses would gain a small-group option; families between 400% and 600% of the poverty level would become newly eligible for premium subsidies; and Medicare beneficiaries would benefit indirectly if government drug-price negotiation lowers prices.

how_it_helps.text: Establishes a public 'Medicare Exchange health plan' that individuals not eligible for Medicare can enroll in through the ACA exchanges, starting in plan year 2021 in selected areas and everywhere in the individual market by plan year 2024.

Directs the Secretary to launch the plan first in rating areas where one or fewer insurers offer exchange plans or where provider shortages and lack of competition drive high costs, including rural and health-professional-shortage areas.

Reimburses providers at Medicare fee-for-service rates, with authority to raise rates up to 25% for services in rural areas, which are generally lower than commercial insurance rates and would hold down premiums.

Eliminates the statutory restriction on the Department of Health and Human Services negotiating prescription drug prices for Medicare, a change that applies to the existing Medicare Part D program immediately upon enactment.
Removes the 400%-of-poverty income cap on ACA premium tax credits, extending subsidies on a sliding scale up to a 13% premium contribution for households at 600% of poverty and above.

Appropriates $1 billion to establish the plan and authorizes $10 billion per year for fiscal 2021-2023 to pool the costs of the highest-cost patients nationwide, reducing premiums for everyone buying individual coverage.

Authorizes grants to community organizations, schools, and health agencies to build partnerships and data systems linking health care with food, housing, transportation, and income assistance, and requires telehealth integration for remote areas.

analysis.who_pays: Private health insurers would lose exchange customers to the public plan; hospitals and physicians would be paid Medicare rates, which are lower than what commercial insurers pay, unless they opt out; and taxpayers would fund the $1 billion startup fund, $10 billion per year in reinsurance, and the expanded premium subsidies.

drawbacks.text: Hospitals and doctors would be paid at Medicare rates, which are lower than commercial rates, and providers enrolled in Medicare or Medicaid would have to join the public plan unless they affirmatively opt out — critics of Medicare-rate public options argue this squeezes providers, particularly financially fragile rural hospitals, though the bill allows up to 25% higher rural payment rates.

The expanded subsidies and reinsurance program carry real taxpayer costs: the bill appropriates $1 billion for the plan's reserve fund, authorizes $10 billion a year for three years of reinsurance, and extends premium credits to households well above the middle-class income level where ACA subsidies currently stop.
Because providers can opt out of the public plan, networks in some areas could be narrower than private plans that pay more, limiting which doctors and hospitals patients can use.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill pairs its main benefit — a lower-cost public option and extended subsidies — with genuine taxpayer costs and a real tradeoff for providers, who would face Medicare-rate payments or have to leave the plan. The reinsurance and rural rate provisions soften some of the pressure on premiums and rural hospitals. On balance it is a substantial expansion of affordable coverage whose main costs fall on insurers, hospitals, and the federal budget rather than on enrollees.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Finance Committee, which never took it up, and it died when the 116th Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Sen. Michael Bennet introduced the bill on April 2, 2019, joined by 11 Democratic cosponsors, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance.
No further action appears in the bill's history: the Finance Committee never held a markup or vote, and the bill never reached the Senate floor.
The 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021, and the bill expired without a vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Private health insurers, hospital systems, and drug makers are better off: the public plan, Medicare-rate payment structure, and government drug-price negotiation never advanced, so no new competitor or rate pressure took effect during this Congress.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Private insurers, hospitals, and drug makers

for.name: Sen. Michael Bennet
for.role: U.S. Senator from Colorado; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Medicare-X Choice Act of 2019 to create a public health plan option on the ACA exchanges.

for.name: 11 Democratic Senate cosponsors
for.role: Cosponsors (Sens. Kaine, Cardin, Klobuchar, Leahy, Smith, Stabenow, Harris, Booker, Peters, Durbin, and Shaheen)
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill as original cosponsors at introduction.

against.name: Sen. Chuck Grassley
against.what_they_did: The Finance Committee, which he chaired, took no action after referral: the bill received no markup, no vote, and never left committee.

against.name: Private health insurance and hospital industry groups
against.role: Industry opponents of a public option
against.what_they_did: Publicly opposed Medicare-rate public option proposals as unfair government competition with private plans and lower payments to providers.

sides.party_line_note: All 12 sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats; no Republican supported the bill, and it died in the Republican-chaired Senate Finance Committee without any committee or floor vote.

industries.note: The public plan would compete directly with private exchange plans at Medicare reimbursement rates, which insurers argued would undercut them and pull customers away; but the bill also authorizes $10 billion a year in reinsurance to pool high-cost patient costs, which would lower private insurers' claims and premiums. The main long-run effect is a new government competitor, which is why insurers opposed it.

Providers in the public plan would be paid at Medicare rates, which are below commercial rates, and Medicare/Medicaid-enrolled providers would have to participate unless they opted out. Hospitals and doctors groups have consistently opposed Medicare-rate public options for this reason, though the bill allows 25% higher rural rates.

The bill strikes the federal ban on HHS negotiating Medicare drug prices, giving the government immediate negotiating authority over Part D drugs — a provision the pharmaceutical industry has long fought.

industries.industry: Community health organizations and educational institutions
industries.note: A new grant program would fund community needs assessments, social-service partnerships, and data systems linking health care with housing, food, and transportation assistance.
